name: Brushing technique (boar bristle)

lead: A boar bristle brush uses tightly spaced natural bristles to smooth and style hair. People use it for smoother, shinier-looking hair, and fans say brushing carries scalp oil down the strands.

Tight bristles create tension while brushing that smooths the hair, and the smoothing is a styling effect you see straight away. The oil-distribution idea comes from hair-care communities; reference sources on hairbrushes do not describe oil distribution, and no studies of the effect were found.

paras: People brush from scalp to ends through dry hair, often daily and sometimes before styling or in a wave or slicked-back routine. The look of smoothness appears immediately, and shine claims build with regular use. Other brush designs, such as cushion and detangler brushes, are made to reduce breakage.
Hairbrush references list no specific hazards. Brushing hard or on tangled hair can pull or break strands, which is why detangler designs exist.

angle.text: Boar bristle brushes smooth hair, and fans say they also spread scalp oil along the strands for added shine. The smoothing is a styling effect you see straight away; the oil-distribution claim has not been tested.

lead: Boar bristle brushing means using a hairbrush with natural boar-hair bristles to smooth, style and add sheen to hair. Such brushes are described as having tightly spaced bristles that increase tension while brushing in order to smooth the hair, and cushion versions are used for detangling [1]. People use them to get a neater, glossier-looking finish on straight or slightly wavy hair before or after styling.

Hair-care communities commonly say that brushing carries natural scalp oil (sebum) down the length of the hair, which gives a smoother, shinier look and can make greasy roots look less obvious. A member of the T Nation forum, for example, described brushing with a boar bristle brush while sectioning hair to spread sebum from scalp to length [2]. Reference sources on hairbrushes describe the smoothing design but do not discuss oil distribution, and no clinical studies of this effect were found [1].
How a brush behaves depends on hair type and condition: Wikipedia notes that straight hair typically looks smoother when brushed, while curly hair tends to expand when brushed dry [1].
infobox: Boar, horsehair, nylon, stainless steel, goat [1]

paras: Hairbrushes include round, vent, cushion, paddle and detangler designs, and bristles may be boar, horsehair, nylon, steel or goat hair; handles are made from woods or plastics [1]. Cushion, paddle and detangler designs are intended to reduce breakage during detangling [1].
An 1854 US patent granted to Hugh Rock is cited as the earliest for a modern hairbrush; later patents include Samuel Firey in 1870 and Lyda D. Newman in 1898 [1].

Conditioning products are described as working by reducing friction between strands so hair combs more smoothly [3]. An undamaged cuticle is coated with a lipid film that lowers friction, and weathering, bleaching and heat styling can strip it [3]. Proponents of boar bristle brushing say the brush moves natural oils from scalp to ends, but reference sources do not report this [1].

Brushing is discussed alongside hair-care routines for smoothness and shine. A general hairstyling reference describes the old "100 strokes a day" rule as outdated [4]. On T Nation, one poster described spreading scalp sebum to the lengths about once every ten days and using a boar bristle brush, sectioned like flat-ironing, when the hair felt greasy [2].

lore.intro: Boar bristle brushes come up in grooming discussions as a tool for smoothing hair and moving scalp oil; the claims are anecdotal [2].
